<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:hard}
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a set of moves on petal permutations, each of which preserves the knot type. A petal permutation $p$ of the unknot with $N$ petals is \emph{$\mathcal{M}$-hard} if there is no sequence of moves in $\mathcal{M}$ from $p$ to the one-petal permutation $(\,0\,)$ all of whose intermediate permutations have at most $N$ petals. The \emph{excess} $e_\mathcal{M}(p)$ is the smallest $E\ge 0$ such that there is such a sequence all of whose intermediate permutations have at most $N+E$ petals.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- thma-1: body_md -->
Every petal permutation of the unknot with at most $7$ petals can be reduced to $(\,0\,)$ by crossing exchanges and trivial petal deletions only. In particular no such permutation is $\mathcal{M}$-hard.
<!-- end thma-1 -->
<!-- thmb-1: body_md -->
Among the $8!=40320$ petal permutations with $9$ petals (counted up to cyclic rotation), $24992$ represent the unknot and exactly $108$ are $\mathcal{M}$-hard. They form six orbits of size $18$ under the dihedral group generated by $\mathsf{R}$ and $\mathsf{S}$, and three orbits up to mirror image, with representatives
\[
\alpha=(\,0\,2\,4\,1\,5\,7\,3\,8\,6\,),\qquad
\beta=(\,0\,2\,5\,3\,8\,1\,7\,4\,6\,),\qquad
\gamma=(\,0\,2\,4\,7\,3\,8\,6\,1\,5\,).
\]
Each of the $108$ permutations is \emph{rigid}: no crossing exchange and no trivial petal deletion applies to it. Consequently $9$ is the smallest number of petals of an $\mathcal{M}$-hard petal permutation.
<!-- end thmb-1 -->
<!-- thmc-1: body_md -->
The hard permutations in the orbits of $\alpha$, $\beta$ and their mirror images have excess $2$. The hard permutations in the orbit of $\gamma$ and of its mirror image have excess $4$: the set of all permutations reachable from $\gamma$ by moves in $\mathcal{M}$ through permutations with at most $11$ petals is finite, has exactly $3186$ elements ($18$ with $9$ petals and $3168$ with $11$ petals), and contains none with fewer than $9$ petals.
<!-- end thmc-1 -->
<!-- construction-1: body_md -->
\label{con:arc}
Use cylindrical coordinates $(r,\theta,z)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, and let the $z$-axis be the \emph{binding}. For $k\in\mathbb{Z}/N$ let $H_k$ be the open half-plane $\theta=2\pi k/N$, the $k$-th \emph{page}. Put
\[
c_j \;=\; j(n+1)\bmod N\qquad (j\in\mathbb{Z}/N).
\]
Let $v_j$ be the point of the binding at height $z=p_j$, and let $A_j$ be a simple arc in $H_k\cup\{\text{binding}\}$ with $k=c_j$, joining $v_j$ to $v_{j+1}$ and meeting the binding only in its endpoints. The \emph{knot of $p$} is $K(p)=\bigcup_j A_j$.
<!-- end construction-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:petalarc}
$K(p)$ is isotopic to the knot represented by the petal diagram with petal permutation $p$, the heights being read in the order in which the knot traverses the strands through the multi-crossing.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Place the multi-crossing of a petal diagram at the origin of the projection plane, viewed along the $z$-axis, with petal $k$ centred at angle $2\pi k/N$ and bounded by two radial edges at angles $2\pi k/N\pm\pi/(2N)$. The strand at height $h$ is a straight segment through the origin. A line through the origin leaving petal $k$ along its counterclockwise edge arrives at angle $2\pi k/N+\pi/(2N)+\pi = 2\pi(k+n+1)/N-\pi/(2N)$. This is the clockwise edge of petal $k+n+1$. Hence, following the knot, consecutive petals differ by $n+1$, which matches the page sequence $c_j$.

The part of the knot between two consecutive passes through the multi-crossing, at heights $p_j$ and $p_{j+1}$, lies in a thin wedge around the angle $2\pi c_j/N$ that no other part of the knot enters, except along the $z$-axis at other heights. An isotopy supported in these wedges flattens each petal, together with the two half-strands bounding it, into the half-plane $H_{c_j}$. The result is $K(p)$. The converse construction is the same isotopy run backwards.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
This is the petal arc presentation of \cite[\S3]{Adams1}. The convention agrees with that of \cite{CGHS}. For instance, their permutations $(\,3\,1\,4\,2\,0\,)$ and $(\,6\,4\,2\,0\,3\,5\,1\,)$ give the trefoil and the figure-eight knot, and both of their moves preserve the knot type of $K(p)$ in all of the more than $1200$ random instances we tested. Conventions differing by the direction of the height axis, or of the traversal, replace $K(p)$ by its mirror image. Since the unknot is amphichiral, and since mirroring maps our move set $\mathcal{M}$ to itself (Remark~\ref{rem:mirror}), none of our results depends on these conventions.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:grid}
Blowing up the binding turns $K(p)$ into a grid (rectangular) diagram \cite{Cromwell,Dynnikov,OSS}. Column $k$ is page $k$ and row $h$ is height $h$. The vertical segment in column $c_j$ joins rows $p_j$ and $p_{j+1}$, and the horizontal segment in row $p_{j+1}$ joins columns $c_j$ and $c_{j+1}$. Vertical segments cross over horizontal ones. Figure~\ref{fig:grid} shows the grid diagram of $\gamma$. This is the form we use in the computations.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Let $p=(\,4\,2\,0\,6\,5\,1\,3\,)$ and $b=6$. Then $P_6=\{\{0,1\},\{2,3\},\{4,5\}\}$ with value sets $\{2,4\},\{0,6\},\{1,5\}$. With $m=1$, $w=4$, $\Delta=\{4,5\}$, $\Delta'=\{0,1\}$ the hypotheses hold, since $[3,3]$ is disjoint from $\{0,6\}$. Thus $\mathsf{X}(6,1,4)$ gives $(\,5\,1\,0\,6\,4\,2\,3\,)$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
$K(\mathsf{R}(p))$ is isotopic to $K(p)$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Compactify $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $S^3$. The binding becomes an unknotted circle and the pages become the pages of an open book with disk pages. An arc presentation in $S^3$ is determined up to isotopy by the cyclic order of its vertices on the binding circle and the cyclic order of its pages \cite{Cromwell}. Sliding the top vertex, at height $N-1$, up through $\infty$ and back from below, carrying its two arcs along in their pages, changes the linear order of the heights by the cyclic shift $h\mapsto h+1 \pmod N$. It leaves the pages unchanged.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
$K(\mathsf{S}(p))$ is isotopic to $K(p)$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Apply the rotation $\rho(x,y,z)=(x,-y,-z)$, by $\pi$ about the $x$-axis. It maps the height $h$ to $-h$, which after relabelling is $N-1-h$, and the page $H_k$ to $H_{-k}$. The arc $A_j$ in page $c_j=j(n+1)$ is mapped to an arc in page $-j(n+1)=c_{-j}$ joining heights $N-1-p_j$ and $N-1-p_{j+1}$. Hence $\rho(K(p))=K(q)$ with $q_{-j}=N-1-p_{j+1}$, which is $\mathsf{S}(p)$ up to cyclic shift.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:mirror}
By the same computation, reversing the word (reflection $\theta\mapsto-\theta$) and complementing the letters (reflection $z\mapsto -z$) each give the mirror image. We verified this on the trefoil using the writhe of a minimal diagram. Mirroring conjugates each of $\mathsf{T}^\pm,\mathsf{X},\mathsf{R},\mathsf{S}$ to a move of the same type, so the set of $\mathcal{M}$-hard words and the excess are invariant under mirroring. One checks that $\mathsf{S}\mathsf{R}\mathsf{S}^{-1}=\mathsf{R}^{-1}$, so $\langle\mathsf{R},\mathsf{S}\rangle$ is dihedral of order $2N$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:CGHS}
Two petal permutations represent isotopic knots if and only if they are related by a finite sequence of trivial petal additions, trivial petal deletions and crossing exchanges.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Results A--C do not rely on Theorem~\ref{thm:CGHS}. They use only that each move in $\mathcal{M}$ preserves the knot type. For $\mathsf{T}^\pm$ and $\mathsf{X}$ this is the easier half of \cite{CGHS}, proved there in Corollary~5 and Lemma~6; for $\mathsf{R},\mathsf{S}$ it was shown above. The completeness statement is used only to guarantee that untangling sequences exist at all, and our explicit sequences make even this unnecessary for the examples.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Every rectangular diagram of the unknot can be transformed into the trivial diagram by a finite sequence of exchange moves and destabilizations. In particular there are no hard rectangular diagrams of the unknot.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:noexchange}
Let $p$ be a petal word with $N=2n+1\ge5$ petals, viewed as the arc presentation $K(p)$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em]
\item[(a)] Let $0\le h\le N-2$. If the letters $h$ and $h+1$ are not cyclically adjacent in $p$, then the page pairs at the vertices of heights $h$ and $h+1$ interleave, so exchanging these vertices is not an exchange move of type (ii). If they are adjacent, then $\mathsf{T}^{-}$ applies to $p$.
\item[(b)] No page exchange (i), stabilization or destabilization transforms $K(p)$ into a petal arc presentation.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
(a) The vertex $v_j$ is the endpoint of the arcs $A_{j-1}$ and $A_j$, in pages $c_{j-1}=c_j+n$ and $c_j$. So its page pair is the chord $\chi_j=\{c_j,\,c_j+n\}$ of the $N$-gon $\mathbb{Z}/N$. Consider two such chords $\{a,a+n\}$ and $\{a+k,a+k+n\}$ with $1\le k\le 2n$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
\item If $1\le k\le n-1$, then $a+k$ lies strictly inside the arc from $a$ to $a+n$, while $a+k+n$ lies outside it. So the chords interleave.
\item If $n+2\le k\le 2n$, then $a+k$ lies outside that arc, while $a+k+n=a+(k-n-1)$ lies inside. So the chords interleave.
\item If $k\in\{n,n+1\}$, the chords share an endpoint.
\end{itemize}
Since $c_i-c_j=(i-j)(n+1)$, sharing an endpoint happens exactly when $i-j=\pm1$, i.e.\ when the two vertices are consecutive along the knot. If $p_i=h$ and $p_j=h+1$ are consecutive along the knot, the letters $h,h+1$ are adjacent in $p$, and $\mathsf{T}^{-}$ applies.

(b) Stabilizations and destabilizations change the number of arcs by one, and petal arc presentations have an odd number of arcs. Now suppose a page exchange swaps two adjacent pages $k,k+1$. The pages visited along the knot become $\tau(c_j)$, where $\tau$ is the transposition $(k\ k{+}1)$ of $\mathbb{Z}/N$. For the result to be a petal arc presentation, for some starting point and orientation, $j\mapsto\tau(c_j)$ would have to be an affine function $j\mapsto u+ js$ with $s\in\{n,n+1\}$. Then $\tau$ itself would be affine. But an affine bijection of $\mathbb{Z}/N$ fixing the two points $k+2,k+3$ (distinct from $k,k+1$ because $N\ge5$) is the identity, since they differ by the unit $1$. This contradicts $\tau\neq\mathrm{id}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:criterion}
Suppose that no unknot word with fewer than $N$ petals is $\mathcal{M}$-hard. Then an unknot word $p$ with $N$ petals is $\mathcal{M}$-hard if and only if no word in the component of $p$ in $G_N$ admits a move $\mathsf{T}^{-}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
A sequence of moves starting at $p$ that never exceeds $N$ petals stays in the component of $p$ until it first applies $\mathsf{T}^{-}$. If some word in the component admits $\mathsf{T}^{-}$, we reach a word with $N-2$ petals, which can then be untangled by hypothesis without exceeding $N-2$ petals.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:TX}
For the smaller move set $\{\mathsf{T}^\pm,\mathsf{X}\}$ of \cite{CGHS}, the same computation finds $264$ hard unknot words with $9$ petals, in $222$ components of the graph generated by $\mathsf{X}$. Of these words, $180$ admit no crossing exchange at all. Result~A holds for this move set as well.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:robust}
Let $\mathcal{M}'$ be any set of moves each of which is a composite of moves in $\mathcal{M}$ passing only through words with at most $N+2$ petals, where $N$ is the number of petals at the start of the composite. Then $\gamma$ is $(\mathcal{M}\cup\mathcal{M}')$-hard.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
A sequence of moves of $\mathcal{M}\cup\mathcal{M}'$ from $\gamma$ through words with at most $9$ petals expands to a sequence of moves of $\mathcal{M}$ through words with at most $11$ petals. By Result~C such a sequence never leaves the closed set described there.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Is the excess of unknot petal diagrams bounded by a function of the number of petals, and how fast must such a function grow? Does the maximal excess over $N$-petal diagrams tend to infinity?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
Is there a natural finite collection of \emph{local} petal-number-preserving moves, beyond crossing exchanges, with respect to which petal diagrams of the unknot admit monotonic simplification, in the spirit of Dynnikov's theorem? By Corollary~\ref{cor:robust}, such moves cannot all be composites passing through only two additional petals.
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
How common are hard diagrams? With $9$ petals, $108$ of the $24992$ unknot words (about $0.43\%$) are $\mathcal{M}$-hard. What is the proportion for larger $N$, for instance in the Petaluma model \cite{EHLN1,EHLN2}?
<!-- end question-3 -->
<!-- question-4: body_md -->
For a non-trivial knot $K$, are there petal diagrams of $K$ that cannot be reduced to a diagram with $p(K)$ petals without first increasing the number of petals? Dynnikov's theorem has no analogue of this kind for arbitrary knots in the rectangular setting either, so the question is whether petal diagrams behave even worse.
<!-- end question-4 -->
